Request renewal of eth0 through systemd-networkd

subject: ITCS217

leftItems: Select the device and forwarding identity for local host-to-host frame delivery
Select the device and forwarding identity for communication between networks
Forward a known unicast frame whose destination is MAC-BB
Select the illustrated lower-metric route to the stated destination
rightItems: Switch: layer-2 frames and destination MAC addresses
Router: layer-3 packets and destination IP addresses

Routers link networks and select forwarding paths using network-layer destination information.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: Two ordinary switched Ethernet LANs are connected by a router. There is no configured broadcast forwarding or bridging across the router. Host A sends an Ethernet broadcast on the first LAN. Which statement correctly describes its scope?
explanation: An ordinary switch forwards within its LAN broadcast domain; a router separates those LAN domains and routes between networks. This does not claim that every switch configuration has one domain.
answers: It automatically reaches both LANs because routers forward every frame.
It stays within the first LAN broadcast domain; reaching another network requires routed communication.
It reaches only the switch and can never reach another host.
The router forwards that Ethernet broadcast unchanged only onto directly attached LANs.
optionExplanations: The stated router does not bridge or forward these Ethernet broadcasts.
The broadcast belongs to the first LAN; routers connect separate networks.
The switch can forward a broadcast to other local hosts.
Direct attachment does not make the router bridge those Ethernet broadcast domains; no such forwarding is configured in the stated scenario.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: Interpret the ordinary Ethernet/IPv4 ARP capture excerpts on PDF pages 56–57. Match each record to its operation, Ethernet destination and meaning; assume no proxy or gratuitous ARP. Match each left item to one right option. Use each right option at most once; some options may be unused.
explanation: The request capture advertises the requester’s own MAC/IP, specifies target IP 10.34.10.80 and leaves target hardware zero. Its ARP operation is 1 and enclosing Ethernet destination is broadcast. The reply capture advertises 10.34.10.80 at 00:26:73:8c:b4:fd and targets the original requester, 10.34.10.44 at 8c:16:45:d6:44:ab. Its operation is 2 and Ethernet destination is unicast to that requester.
leftItems: Request excerpt: sender hardware 8c:16:45:d6:44:ab; sender protocol 10.34.10.44; target hardware 00:00:00:00:00:00; target protocol 10.34.10.80
Reply excerpt: sender hardware 00:26:73:8c:b4:fd; sender protocol 10.34.10.80; target hardware 8c:16:45:d6:44:ab; target protocol 10.34.10.44
rightItems: Operation 1; broadcast Ethernet destination FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF; asks who owns 10.34.10.80
Operation 1; unicast to 00:26:73:8c:b4:fd; asks for the requester’s own IPv4 address
pairExplanations: The request capture advertises the requester’s own MAC/IP, specifies target IP 10.34.10.80 and leaves target hardware zero. Its ARP operation is 1 and enclosing Ethernet destination is broadcast.

The reply capture advertises 10.34.10.80 at 00:26:73:8c:b4:fd and targets the original requester, 10.34.10.44 at 8c:16:45:d6:44:ab. Its operation is 2 and Ethernet destination is unicast to that requester.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: For the Ethernet/IPv4 ARP format illustrated in the lecture, match each descriptor to its value. Interpret the values as protocol fields, not Ethernet destination addresses. Match each left item to one right option. Use each right option at most once; some options may be unused.
explanation: Hardware type 0x0001 denotes Ethernet in the illustrated format. Protocol type 0x0800 identifies IPv4. Ethernet hardware addresses occupy six bytes. IPv4 protocol addresses occupy four bytes.
leftItems: Hardware type
Protocol type
Hardware address length
Protocol address length
pairExplanations: Hardware type 0x0001 denotes Ethernet in the illustrated format.
Protocol type 0x0800 identifies IPv4.
Ethernet hardware addresses occupy six bytes.
IPv4 protocol addresses occupy four bytes.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: In the ordinary Ethernet/IPv4 request, A (IP A-IP, MAC A-MAC) asks for B-IP on its LAN. The Ethernet frame destination is FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF. explanation: The sender hardware field identifies A’s MAC. The sender protocol field identifies A’s IPv4 address. The illustrated unknown target hardware field is zero; it is different from the enclosing Ethernet broadcast destination. The request asks for the owner of B-IP, so B-IP is the target protocol value.
leftItems: Sender hardware address
Sender protocol address
Target hardware address in the illustrated request
Target protocol address
pairExplanations: The sender hardware field identifies A’s MAC.
The sender protocol field identifies A’s IPv4 address.
The illustrated unknown target hardware field is zero; it is different from the enclosing Ethernet broadcast destination.
The request asks for the owner of B-IP, so B-IP is the target protocol value.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: B (B-IP, B-MAC) replies to the ordinary ARP request from A (A-IP, A-MAC) on the same Ethernet LAN. Match the four address fields INSIDE B’s ARP reply. Match each left item to one right option. Use each right option at most once; some options may be unused.
explanation: B sends the reply, so sender hardware is B-MAC. B’s advertised IPv4 address is B-IP. The reply targets requester A’s known MAC, A-MAC. The target protocol address identifies requester A-IP.

Sender protocol address
Target hardware address
Target protocol address
pairExplanations: B sends the reply, so sender hardware is B-MAC.
B’s advertised IPv4 address is B-IP.
The reply targets requester A’s known MAC, A-MAC.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: Match each Windows/Linux ARP-cache task to the correct result or command. The example arp -a record is 10.0.2.2 at 52:54:00:12:35:00 on eth0. Match each left item to one right option. Use each right option at most once; some options may be unused.
explanation: arp -a exposes the cached protocol-address to hardware-address association for the interface. The lecture shows netsh interface ip delete arpcache as an administrative cache-deletion operation; arp -d is also shown for deletion.

pairExplanations: arp -a exposes the cached protocol-address to hardware-address association for the interface.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: Follow Alice→R1→R2→Bob in the lecture. Each relevant hop here is an Ethernet-capable local link; required ARP caches are initially empty. Match each forwarding stage to the action needed. explanation: For an off-network destination, Alice builds a local frame to her default gateway, not directly to Bob’s distant MAC. R1 needs R2’s adjacent-interface MAC for this explicitly Ethernet-capable hop. Only the last-hop router on Bob’s LAN needs Bob’s MAC for this delivery; earlier nodes use their own local next hops. Bob decapsulates the local frame to obtain the enclosed datagram.
leftItems: Alice sends toward off-network Bob through local gateway R1
R1 forwards across its local Ethernet-capable link to R2
R2 forwards on the final LAN containing Bob
Bob receives the frame addressed to his local interface
rightItems: Resolve Bob’s local IP to Bob’s MAC; earlier hops needed only their own next-hop MACs
Remove the incoming link frame and pass its enclosed datagram upward
Resolve the local gateway interface IP to R1’s local MAC
Resolve the next-router interface IP to R2’s MAC on their shared link
Every node first resolves Bob’s MAC end-to-end
pairExplanations: For an off-network destination, Alice builds a local frame to her default gateway, not directly to Bob’s distant MAC.
R1 needs R2’s adjacent-interface MAC for this explicitly Ethernet-capable hop.
Only the last-hop router on Bob’s LAN needs Bob’s MAC for this delivery; earlier nodes use their own local next hops.
Bob decapsulates the local frame to obtain the enclosed datagram.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: Match the two address-resolution needs to the appropriate mechanism. Use the stated purpose and server-table behavior; do not infer an IP header from the simplified RARP illustration. Match each left item to one right option. Use each right option at most once; some options may be unused.
explanation: ARP resolves the adjacent target protocol address to a hardware address for local transmission. RARP answers the reverse own-address question using the requester MAC and a server mapping table; this differs from asking for a next-hop MAC.
leftItems: A sender knows its next hop’s IPv4 address but needs the local-link hardware address
A booting station knows its own hardware address but needs its assigned IPv4 address
rightItems: RARP: a server consults its MAC-to-IP table and returns the requester’s assigned IP
ARP: resolve the known local next-hop IPv4 address to its MAC
ARP: obtain the requester’s own assigned IP from a server MAC-to-IP table
pairExplanations: ARP resolves the adjacent target protocol address to a hardware address for local transmission.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: A laptop sends an IP datagram over Wi-Fi to a router, which forwards it onto an Ethernet link. What must happen at the router?
answers: Forward the complete Wi-Fi frame unchanged onto Ethernet
Remove the Wi-Fi frame and put the datagram into a new Ethernet frame
Discard the datagram because different links cannot form one path
Keep the Wi-Fi header and add only an Ethernet trailer
explanation: Frame encapsulation is local to each link. The datagram is forwarded in a frame suitable for the next link.
optionExplanations: Wi-Fi and Ethernet use different link-specific frame formats.
The router decapsulates the incoming frame and constructs the outgoing link frame.
A path can combine different link technologies.
The outgoing link needs its own suitable frame, not a hybrid header/trailer.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: A receiver reports that new frames are dropped because its buffer is full. The link has no observed bit corruption. Which change directly addresses the stated problem?
answers: Increase the number of error-detection bits only
Change the destination MAC to broadcast
Coordinate the sending rate with receiver capacity
Replace every data frame with a link-management frame
explanation: This is a flow-control problem: the sender must adapt to receiver capacity to avoid overflow.
optionExplanations: Detection bits do not create receiver buffer capacity.
Broadcasting does not regulate arrival rate at this receiver.
Flow control prevents the sender from overwhelming the receiver.
Management frames do not provide the required data-flow regulation by themselves.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: A dedicated full-duplex link has no shared-medium contention. A capture still shows each datagram enclosed by link control fields. Which conclusion explains this observation?
answers: Framing serves link delivery even when contention coordination is unnecessary
The capture proves a collision must have occurred
The link must actually be a shared bus because frames are present
A dedicated link should carry only application bytes without link control fields
explanation: The data-link sublayer still frames datagrams on dedicated links. Shared-medium access coordination addresses a separate concern.
optionExplanations: The need to encapsulate data and carry link control information remains on a dedicated link.
Frame presence does not establish a collision.
Both dedicated and shared links use framing.
Dedicated access does not remove the need for link framing.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: A receiver identifies a damaged frame. It has error detection but no forward error correction. Which inference about recovery is justified?
answers: The detection result itself uniquely reconstructs the original bits
Detecting the error guarantees that retransmission has already happened
Detecting the error guarantees that this link implements recovery
The damage is identified, but detection alone does not establish correction or retransmission
explanation: Detection establishes that corruption was identified. It does not imply receiver-side correction or guarantee optional ACK/retransmission support.
optionExplanations: Error detection does not itself reconstruct the original data.
A detection result does not prove that the sender has retransmitted.
The lecture marks link recovery as optional.
Detection, receiver correction and link recovery are distinct capabilities.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: Three HDLC traces show: X, a secondary sends only after primary permission; Y, a secondary initiates while a primary still manages the link; Z, either peer combined station initiates. Which mode assignment fits all three traces?
answers: X: ARM; Y: NRM; Z: ABM
X: NRM; Y: ARM; Z: ABM
X: NRM; Y: ABM; Z: ARM
X: ABM; Y: ARM; Z: NRM
explanation: The traces differ in permission and station roles: NRM is permission-controlled, ARM retains primary management while allowing secondary initiation, and ABM is balanced.
optionExplanations: This reverses the permission distinction between NRM and ARM.
NRM requires permission, ARM permits secondary initiation, and ABM uses balanced peers.
ABM is the peer arrangement Z, not the unbalanced arrangement Y.
NRM is the permission-controlled arrangement X, not balanced peer operation Z.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: Use the illustrated HDLC variant with two 8-bit flags, an 8-bit address, an 8-bit control field and a 32-bit FCS. With a 120-byte payload, what is the total frame length, excluding any bit stuffing?
answers: 124 bytes
126 bytes
128 bytes
152 bytes

Six bytes would fit a 16-bit rather than the specified 32-bit FCS.
The overhead is 1+1+1+1+4=8 bytes; 120+8=128 bytes.
The 32-bit FCS occupies four bytes, not 32 bytes.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: A capture decoder must distinguish two HDLC-like formats. One adds a Protocol field for upper-layer identification; the other adds a Type field. Which pairing is correct?

LAPB: Protocol; basic HDLC: Type

ATM and Frame Relay have different depicted structures.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: In the lecture’s routed path, Alice sends to Bob through R1 and R2. Assume no address translation. Which identities remain the datagram’s endpoints while local link addresses change?
answers: The MAC addresses of R1 and R2
The IP addresses of Alice and Bob

End-host MAC addresses do not serve as the frame endpoints on all intermediate links.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: A service gives several servers the same service destination and delivers each request to just one member of that set. Which delivery pattern does this describe?
answers: Broadcast
Multicast
Unicast to every member
Anycast

optionExplanations: Broadcast delivers to everyone in the broadcast domain.

Anycast means delivery to one of multiple possible receivers.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: A Windows ipconfig /all listing shows IPv4 Address 192.168.43.222, Subnet Mask 255.255.255.0, Default Gateway 192.168.43.1 and DHCP Server 192.168.43.1. Which field identifies the next-hop router for off-network traffic?
answers: IPv4 Address
Subnet Mask
Default Gateway
DHCP Server solely because it allocated the address

optionExplanations: The IPv4 Address field identifies the host interface.

The Default Gateway field identifies the router used for off-network destinations.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: A client has received an address proposal from a DHCP server. It now sends the message selecting that proposal, but has not yet received the server’s final confirmation. Which pair describes those next two message roles?
answers: Discover selects; Offer confirms
Offer selects; Discover confirms

optionExplanations: Discover seeks configuration and Offer proposes it.
Offer is a server proposal, while Discover is a client solicitation.

The client Request selects the proposal and the server ACK confirms it.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: A switch table maps MAC 02:00:00:00:00:11 to port 2, 02:00:00:00:00:22 to port 5, and 02:00:00:00:00:33 to port 7. A frame arrives on port 2 with destination 02:00:00:00:00:33. Which output port follows from the supplied table?
answers: Port 7
Port 2
Port 5
All listed ports because the destination is known

Port 2 is associated with another MAC and is the ingress port.
Port 5 maps to the address ending in 22.
A known unicast mapping supplies the specific destination port.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: An ordinary Ethernet/IPv4 ARP request has destination Ethernet MAC FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF and target hardware address 00:00:00:00:00:00 in the ARP payload. Why are those fields different?
answers: The zero field makes the Ethernet frame unicast
The Ethernet destination broadcasts the query; the ARP target MAC is still unknown
The all-ones field identifies only the DHCP server

The broadcast reaches local stations, while zeros represent the unresolved target hardware address in the illustrated request.
The broadcast MAC addresses the broadcast domain, not a particular DHCP server.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: Alice sends through R1 to R2, and Bob is on R2’s directly connected Ethernet LAN. No relevant ARP mapping is cached. Who must resolve Bob’s IP to Bob’s MAC for the final hop?
answers: Alice before sending to R1
R1 before sending to R2
R2 on Bob’s LAN
Every router must resolve Bob’s MAC on its own LAN
explanation: Each hop resolves its own local next-hop address. Bob’s MAC is needed by R2 for final-link delivery, not by Alice or R1 for their earlier links.

R2 is the final router on Bob’s LAN and needs Bob’s MAC to construct the last Ethernet frame.
A remote host MAC is not the local next-hop address for every router.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: An older booting station knows its own MAC address but needs its assigned IP address. Which choice distinguishes that task from ordinary ARP?
answers: RARP asks a server for the station’s IP using its known MAC; ARP resolves a known local next-hop IP to a MAC
ARP and RARP both primarily allocate complete DHCP configuration
ARP finds the station’s own IP from its MAC; RARP finds the gateway MAC from its IP
RARP chooses an Internet route while ARP identifies UDP ports
explanation: RARP supports an own-IP lookup based on a known hardware address. Ordinary ARP resolves a known local next-hop protocol address to its hardware address.
optionExplanations: This matches the complementary directions described for RARP and ARP.
DHCP provides broader configuration; these are address-resolution purposes.
This swaps the roles of the two protocols.
Route selection and UDP port identification are different functions.
